analysis.one_liner: Subjected the insurance industry to antitrust laws for price fixing and monopolization, ending a decades-old exemption.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill in October 1994, but the full House never voted on it before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, insurance companies have been exempt from most federal antitrust laws under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, meaning insurers could agree on prices or divide up markets without facing the lawsuits other industries face. This bill would have stripped that exemption for core antitrust violations — price fixing, dividing territories or customers, tying products, and monopolizing — while keeping the exemption for harmless shared activities like compiling historical claims data. The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee in an amended form with many added carve-outs, but it never came up for a vote on the House floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People and businesses who buy insurance. With the exemption gone, insurers who fixed prices, allocated markets, tied products, or monopolized could be sued under the Sherman and Clayton Acts, the same as companies in any other industry — a pressure that tends to push premiums down.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would make federal antitrust laws applicable to the business of insurance for conduct involving price fixing, market allocation, tying arrangements, and monopolization, ending the blanket McCarran-Ferguson exemption for those practices [S2].

The reported version would have let the Justice Department study and report on the law's effect on insurance markets and would have published risk-pool notifications publicly, adding transparency [S3, S4].

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies, which would lose immunity from antitrust lawsuits for price fixing, market division, tying, and monopolization, and could face litigation costs and damages that might be passed through to premiums.

drawbacks.text: Insurers and their state regulators have long argued that joint compilation of loss data and actuarial calculations is essential to pricing insurance accurately, and antitrust liability could chill legitimate cooperation or reduce coverage availability — concerns the bill tried to address by keeping safe harbors for historical loss data, actuarial services, standard policy forms, and risk pools [S2, S3].

The reported version was heavily pared back: it preserved exemptions for loss data, loss development factors, standard forms, insurance manuals, trend factors during a transition period, underwriting capacity risk pools, building inspection programs, and workers' compensation experience rating, so its practical effect on prices would have been narrower than the original bill [S3, S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted genuine antitrust violations — cartels fixing premiums or carving up territories — which is where consumers could gain the most. But the committee version carved out so many safe harbors that the real-world price effect would likely have been modest, and the main benefit would have been putting insurers under the same legal rules as everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Judiciary Committee for over a year and a half, was reported to the House with amendments in October 1994, and was placed on the calendar — but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jack Brooks introduced the bill on January 5, 1993, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S6].

As introduced, it would have ended the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for insurance price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization, while preserving the exemption for sharing historical loss data and actuarial services [S2].
The bill went through subcommittee hearings in July 1993 and subcommittee and full committee markups in July 1994 [S6].

The Judiciary Committee reported an amended version on October 7, 1994 (H. Rept. 103-853), which added broad safe harbors for loss data, standard policy forms, manuals, trend factors during a two-year transition, risk pools, and trade association activities [S3, S6].
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar on October 7, 1994, but the House never voted on it, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S6, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies, which kept their antitrust exemption and remained shielded from lawsuits over price fixing and market allocation; consumers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Jack Brooks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the Judiciary Committee, which he chaired, to a committee report in October 1994.

for.name: Reps. Edwards (CA), Collins (MI), Kopetski (OR), and Johnston (FL)
for.what_they_did: Added their names as additional sponsors in June 1994 as the bill advanced.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, marked up the bill, and reported it to the House with amendments on October 7, 1994.

against.name: Insurance industry
against.role: Insurers benefiting from the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption
against.what_they_did: Opposed narrowing the antitrust exemption; the industry has historically lobbied to preserve McCarran-Ferguson immunity, and the committee version emerged with extensive safe harbors for insurer data-sharing and risk pools.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken on the bill; its sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, but there is no record of how the full House or the committee voted.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped their antitrust immunity for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization, exposing them to the same antitrust liability as other industries. Insurers' interest in keeping the exemption runs against customers, since immunity from cartel liability removes pressure to compete on price.

industries.industry: Insurance agents and their trade associations
industries.note: The bill included a safe harbor allowing national and affiliated state agent trade associations to prepare and share reports on insurer practices without antitrust liability, protecting the agent associations' existing role.

The bill preserved exemptions for collecting and disseminating historical loss data, loss development factors, and actuarial services, keeping the industry's shared data infrastructure intact even as it tightened antitrust rules elsewhere.
